references.text: The context for the arrival at Marah, where Israel wandered three days in the wilderness without finding water.
The solution to the bitter water at Marah, where the Lord showed Moses a tree that made the water drinkable.
The travel route mentioning Marah as one of the places the Israelites camped on their way from Egypt.
Naomi uses the name 'Marah' (bitter) for herself because of her suffering, sharing the same root word as the place name Marah.
Proverbs uses images of water as a metaphor, including the contrast between bitter and sweet water.
Jeremiah describes Israel as having forsaken the Lord, the fountain of living water, to hew out broken cisterns.
James asks whether a spring can yield both fresh and bitter water from the same opening, a parallel to the bitter water at Marah.
Revelation explicitly uses the motif from Exodus concerning bitter water as an image of God's judgment, while Exodus shows how God can remove this bitterness.
